Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how things have felt for you since your baby arrived. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question check-in that helps us see how you’re coping emotionally in these first weeks and months postpartum. Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team; the goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space so we can figure out the best way to support you. We’ll go through one question at a time, talking about how you’ve felt over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, I can still laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my partner makes a silly face or when the dog does something goofy, I’ll catch myself smiling. It just feels like the laughter fades faster than it used to, like I’m enjoying the moment but then my mind drifts right back to worrying about the baby or thinking I should be doing something “productive.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yeah. I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny—like when my sister sent that ridiculous meme—but it feels lighter, shorter… like the happy feeling doesn’t stick around the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do find myself looking forward to little things—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or the short walk we take to the mailbox—but it’s not with the same excitement I used to feel. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” instead of “I can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her stomach, or that I wasn’t soothing her the “right” way. I know, logically, babies just have off days, but I still felt like I must have done something wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of times this week I’ll just be sitting there, everything quiet, and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s too still in the bassinet—even though I can see her breathing on the monitor. I check her and she’s fine, but it’s like my brain needs to invent something to fret over.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more like a quick jolt of “what if something’s wrong?” that passes once I peek at her or pick her up. It’s uncomfortable for a minute, but I can talk myself down pretty fast.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. Like when she won’t settle and the laundry’s piled up, I feel this wave of “I can’t keep up.” It passes once I check off one small task, but in the moment it feels like everything’s stacked too high.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, not really. Once I finally get to bed, I mostly fall asleep okay. It’s just that some nights it takes me a little longer to drift off because my mind keeps replaying the day—wondering if I did enough or if she’s gaining weight like she should—but I wouldn’t say I’m “unhappy to the point of lying awake.”
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel that way sometimes—like yesterday evening, out of nowhere, this heaviness just settled on me. It’s not all day, and I can still smile when the baby grins, but there are moments when I feel kind of empty or on the verge of tears for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Maybe once or twice this week. The worst was two nights ago—she finally went down for a four-hour stretch and instead of sleeping I just sat on the couch and teared up, thinking I’m failing at this mom thing. It didn’t last long, but the tears came without me really planning to cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  Source: Patient self-report (EPDS-style items)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia: diminished intensity/ duration of pleasure (laughing, coffee, walks)  
- Intermittent sad/empty mood, evening heaviness, tearfulness (1–2×/wk)  
- Excessive self-blame re infant care; sense of “failing as a mom”  
- Unwarranted worries (e.g., infant breathing) with transient tachycardia; quickly self-soothed  
- Episodic feeling of being overwhelmed when tasks accumulate; improves with completing one item  
- No sleep-onset problems per se, but ruminating before bed; nil middle-of-night depressive insomnia  
- No self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Mild, intermittent depressive and anxiety symptoms tied to infant-care stressors; no persistent functional impairment or safety concerns.

Screening significance  
- Subsyndromal mood and anxiety symptoms within postpartum context  
- Protective factors: intact reality testing, good infant attachment behaviors, absence of self-harm, able to self-soothe  
- Recommend routine follow-up in 1–2 wk and psychoeducation; if symptoms worsen, persist, or include any self-harm ideation, escalate for formal assessment

Overall: low to mild risk at present; continue monitoring.
